newsitem.title: NORWAY: Storebrand top executive quits after row.
newsitem.headline: Storebrand top executive quits after row.

text.p: An investment executive in Norway's biggest insurance company quit on Thursday because he felt persecuted by media questioning his role in a controversy over alleged trading by portfolio managers for personal gain.
Riulf Rustad, executive vice president of Storebrand Investment Management, which manages the group's securities portfolio, said in a statement he had submitted his resignation.
"I am not interested in a leading position in Storebrand or any other part of society if it means that I am a sitting duck for some journalists," Rustad said. "The price is too high."
"I have not in any way tried to enrich myself through my position in Storebrand," he said.
Storebrand chief executive officer Aage Korsvold, who on Wednesday banned Storebrand portfolio managers from trading shares privately in their work, said he accepted Rustad's resignation with regret.
"We have full confidence in Riulf Rustad," he said.

The announcements followed the resignation on Wednesday of Storebrand Spar investment manager Tore Schoeitz. He left after the Storebrand management said it no longer had confidence in him because he had traded privately allegedly for personal gain.
The row began with a share issue administrered by Platou Securities in Norwegian Applied Technology (NAT), a small offshore company that became listed on the Oslo Bourse last month.
The issue was oversubscribed 13 times and the price eventually grew 150 percent from the orginal level of 6.50 crowns.

Several portfolio managers in insurance companies, including Rustad and Schoeitz, were given the opportunity to buy stock while hundreds of other investors were shut out from the issue, financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv said.
Rustad said he had bought shares in NAT for his personal portfolio but that it was not in conflict with his work because NAT did not fit into his professional investment strategy.
Korsvold said no clients had suffered from the private trade but said it had raised doubt about the ethics of Storebrand investors.
